tracks.name: Express Foundations
tracks.description: Create a server, define routes, and read input from the URL.

lessons.title: 1. Your first server
lessons.summary: An Express app is a request handler you hand to an HTTP server.

activities.title: From app to listening socket
activities.instruction: `express()` creates an application object. The app collects routes and middleware; `app.listen(port)` starts the HTTP server and keeps the process alive.

activities.title: What does listen do?
activities.question: What does `app.listen(3000)` do?
choices: Starts an HTTP server bound to port 3000
activities.answer: Starts an HTTP server bound to port 3000
activities.explanation: Routes describe what to answer. `listen()` opens the port and starts accepting connections.

activities.title: Start a server
activities.instruction: Start an Express server on port 4000 and log 'API ready' once it is listening.

teaching.text: An Express app is a function that receives `(req, res)`. Routes and middleware are stored on it; `app.listen()` hands that function to Node's HTTP server.
`listen()` returns the server object. If you need to close it later — in tests, for example — keep that return value.

lessons.task: Start an Express server on port 4000 and log 'API ready'.
hints: `app.listen(port, callback)` starts the server; the callback runs once the port is open.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does an Express script that only defines routes and never calls listen() exit immediately?

lessons.title: 2. GET routes
lessons.summary: Map a method and path to a handler that writes the response.

activities.title: One route, one response
activities.instruction: `app.get(path, handler)` matches GET requests. The handler must end the response — `res.send()` or `res.json()` — or the client waits forever.

activities.title: Missing response
activities.question: What happens if a route handler never calls `res.send()` or `res.json()`?
choices: The request hangs until it times out
activities.answer: The request hangs until it times out
activities.explanation: Express does not invent a response. If no handler ends the request, the socket stays open until the client or server times out.

activities.title: Add a health check
activities.instruction: Add a GET route for `/health` that responds with the plain text `ok`.

teaching.text: A route is a method plus a path plus a handler. The path is matched exactly unless you add parameters (`:id`) or wildcards.
`res.send()` guesses the content type from the value. Pass an object to `res.json()` when you want JSON explicitly.

lessons.task: Add a GET route for `/health` that responds with `ok`.
lessons.starterCode:
const app = require('./app');

// GET /health should respond with ok
hints: The first argument is the path, the second is the handler.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would you return `res.send('ok')` instead of `res.json({ status: 'ok' })`?

lessons.title: 3. Route parameters
lessons.summary: Turn part of the path into a named value your handler can read.

activities.title: The colon marks a slot
activities.instruction: A `:name` segment in the path becomes a key on `req.params`. The same route handles every id, so the handler can look up the right record.

activities.title: Types in params
activities.question: For `GET /users/42`, what is `req.params.id`?
activities.explanation: URL segments are always strings. Convert with `Number(...)` before comparing to a numeric id.

activities.title: Echo the id
activities.instruction: Add a GET route for `/users/:id` that responds with `{ id }` using the value from the URL.

teaching.text: Everything in a URL is a string. `req.params.id` is `'42'`, not `42`, which matters when your database uses numbers.
Register specific paths like `/users/me` before `/users/:id`, or `me` will be swallowed as an id.

lessons.task: Add a GET route for `/users/:id` that responds with `{ id }`.
lessons.starterCode:
const app = require('./app');

// GET /users/:id should respond with the id from the path
hints: Read the value from `req.params.id` and put it straight into the JSON body.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What happens to a request for `/users/me` if `/users/:id` is registered first?

lessons.title: 4. Query strings
lessons.summary: Optional filters live after the `?`, and every value arrives as a string.

activities.title: Defaults for optional input
activities.instruction: `req.query` holds the parsed query string. Because every field is optional, give each one a default with `||` or `??`.

activities.title: Repeated keys
activities.question: What is `req.query.tag` for `?tag=js&tag=node`?
activities.explanation: Express collects repeated keys into an array. Code that assumes a string breaks the first time a client sends two values.

activities.title: Read a limit
activities.instruction: Add a GET route for `/products` that reads `?limit=`, defaults to 20, and responds with `{ limit }` as a number.

teaching.text: Query strings are for optional modifiers: filtering, sorting, pagination. Path parameters identify a resource; query parameters tune the response.
Clamp user-supplied numbers. `?limit=100000` will happily ask your database for the whole table.

lessons.task: Add a GET route for `/products` that reads `?limit=`, defaults to 20, and responds with `{ limit }`.
lessons.starterCode:
const app = require('./app');

// GET /products?limit=5 should respond with { limit: 5 }
hints: Read `req.query.limit` and convert it with `Number(...)` so the JSON body holds a number.

const limit = Number(req.query.limit) || 20;
res.json({ limit });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is defaulting `limit` safer than trusting whatever number the client sends?

tracks.name: Building REST APIs
tracks.description: Create, update, and delete resources with the right status codes.

lessons.title: 5. Reading JSON bodies
lessons.summary: Express does not parse request bodies until you add the JSON middleware.

activities.title: Opt in to parsing
activities.instruction: `express.json()` is middleware that reads the raw request body, parses JSON, and exposes it as `req.body`. Register it once with `app.use()` before the routes that need it.

activities.title: Without the middleware
activities.question: What is `req.body` in a POST handler if `express.json()` was never registered?
activities.explanation: No parser ran, so there is no body to read. `req.body` stays undefined and `req.body.name` throws a TypeError.

activities.title: Echo the body
activities.instruction: Register the JSON body parser, then add a POST route for `/echo` that responds with `req.body`.

teaching.text: The request body arrives as a stream of bytes. Middleware turns it into an object; without it there is nothing on `req.body`.
`express.json()` only parses `application/json`. Form posts need `express.urlencoded({ extended: true })` as well.

lessons.task: Register `express.json()` and add a POST route for `/echo` that responds with the parsed body.
hints: `app.use(express.json())` goes above the routes.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is body parsing middleware rather than something Express always does?

lessons.title: 6. Creating with POST
lessons.summary: POST creates a resource and answers 201 with what was created.

activities.title: Add and return
activities.instruction: A create handler validates input, stores the new record, and responds with status 201 plus the stored resource so the client learns its id.

activities.title: 201 vs 200
activities.question: Which status best describes a successful POST that created a record?
activities.explanation: 201 says a new resource exists. Include it in the body, or at least a `Location` header pointing at its URL.

activities.title: Create a product
activities.instruction: Add a POST route for `/products` that pushes `req.body` onto the `products` array and responds 201 with the created product.

teaching.text: POST is not idempotent: two identical requests create two resources. PUT and DELETE are expected to be repeatable.
Never spread `req.body` straight into a database write without checking fields. It lets a client set anything your schema allows, including ownership.

lessons.task: Add a POST route for `/products` that stores the body and responds 201.
lessons.starterCode:
const products = [];

// POST /products should store the body and respond 201
hints: Push the new object onto the array, then `res.status(201).json(...)` it back.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does the response body matter to a client that just created a record?

lessons.title: 7. Updating with PUT
lessons.summary: Find the record, change it, or say clearly that it is missing.

activities.title: Find, replace, respond
activities.instruction: Locate the record with `findIndex`, keep its id, replace the rest, and respond with the updated object. If the index is -1, answer 404.

activities.title: No match
activities.question: `findIndex` returns -1. Which response fits best?
activities.explanation: The request was valid; the resource simply isn't there. 400 would blame the client's input, 500 the server.

activities.title: Update a product
activities.instruction: Add a PUT route for `/products/:id` that updates the matching product, responds with it, and answers 404 when no product matches.

teaching.text: PUT means replace the resource with what I sent. PATCH means change only the fields present. Either way the id comes from the URL, never from the body.
Spreading `...req.body` over the record also overwrites the id. Put the id back last, as above.

lessons.task: Add a PUT route for `/products/:id` that updates or returns 404.
lessons.starterCode:
const products = [];

// PUT /products/:id updates one product; 404 if it is missing
hints: Compare `Number(req.params.id)` to each product id with `findIndex`.

const index = products.findIndex((p) => p.id === Number(req.params.id));
if (index === -1) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What breaks if you let the request body decide which record gets updated?

lessons.title: 8. Deleting with DELETE
lessons.summary: Remove the record and answer with no body at all.

activities.title: Splice it out
activities.instruction: `splice(index, 1)` removes one element in place. A successful delete has nothing to say, so respond 204 and stop.

activities.title: Body on a 204
activities.question: A 204 response has `res.json({ ok: true })` attached. What does the client receive?
activities.explanation: 204 is defined as having no content. Sending a body either gets dropped or confuses strict clients; use `res.status(204).end()`.

activities.title: Delete a product
activities.instruction: Add a DELETE route for `/products/:id` that removes the matching product, responds 204, and answers 404 when it is missing.

teaching.text: Deleting is a state change like any other, so it is a normal route — protected by the same auth and ownership checks as an update.
Prefer 204 over `200 { success: true }`. Clients already know a 2xx delete worked from the status.

lessons.task: Add a DELETE route for `/products/:id` that removes the product and responds 204.
lessons.starterCode:
const products = [];

// DELETE /products/:id removes one product and responds 204
hints: Find the index, `splice` it out, then send an empty 204.

products.splice(index, 1);
res.status(204).end();
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should a delete route check ownership before removing a record?

tracks.name: Middleware & Errors
tracks.description: Share logic between routes and fail in a way clients can handle.

lessons.title: 9. Middleware
lessons.summary: Middleware runs before your handler and decides whether to continue.

activities.title: A logger in the pipeline
activities.instruction: Every middleware receives `(req, res, next)`. Calling `next()` passes control to the next layer; never calling it leaves the request hanging.

activities.title: Order matters
activities.question: A route is registered above `app.use(logger)`. Does the logger run for that route?
choices: No — Express runs layers in registration order
activities.answer: No — Express runs layers in registration order
activities.explanation: The stack is ordered. Middleware registered after a route never sees requests the route already answered.

activities.title: Log every request
activities.instruction: Add a middleware that logs the method and URL, then continues, and register it for every request.

teaching.text: Middleware is just a function with three arguments. A request travels through them in order until something responds.
Reading a body or user in middleware only helps routes registered after it — put shared setup at the top of the file.

lessons.task: Write a logger middleware and register it for every request.
lessons.starterCode:
const app = require('./app');

// Log the method and URL of every request, then continue
hints: Register it with `app.use((req, res, next) => { ... })`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What happens to a request if a middleware returns early without calling next() and without responding?

lessons.title: 10. Validation middleware
lessons.summary: Reject bad input in one place instead of in every handler.

activities.title: Reject before the handler
activities.instruction: A validation middleware answers 400 when input is invalid and calls `next()` when it is fine. The route then only sees valid requests.

activities.title: Forgotten return
activities.question: A validator sends a 400 response but does not return, then calls `next()`. What happens?
choices: The 400 is sent and the route still runs
activities.answer: The 400 is sent and the route still runs
activities.explanation: The route still executes, which usually triggers "Cannot set headers after they are sent". Always `return res.status(...)` in middleware.

activities.title: Require a name
activities.instruction: Write a `requireName` middleware that responds 400 with an error when `req.body.name` is missing, otherwise calls `next()`.

teaching.text: Validating in middleware keeps handlers short and guarantees every route using it sees the same rules.
400 tells the client to fix the request. 422 is the alternative when the JSON parsed but the values are semantically wrong.

lessons.task: Write a `requireName` middleware that returns 400 or calls `next()`.
hints: Check the field, return a 400 response, and only call `next()` on the happy path.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why must a validation middleware return after sending an error response?

lessons.title: 11. The error handler
lessons.summary: One place to turn thrown errors into a safe response.

activities.title: Four arguments, last in line
activities.instruction: Express recognises an error handler by its four parameters. Register it after all routes so every `next(err)` and thrown error lands here.

activities.title: Leaking errors
activities.question: Why not send `err.message` and `err.stack` to every client?
choices: They can leak file paths, queries, and internals
activities.answer: They can leak file paths, queries, and internals
activities.explanation: Stack traces and driver errors expose internals to attackers. Log the details server-side; send a generic message.

activities.title: Add a safe error handler
activities.instruction: Add a 4-argument error handler at the end of the app that logs the error and responds 500 with a generic message.

teaching.text: `next(err)` skips every normal middleware and jumps to the error handler. That is how a deep helper can report failure without knowing about HTTP.
The fourth argument must be present even if unused. Remove `next` and Express treats the function as ordinary middleware.

lessons.task: Add an error handler that logs the failure and responds 500.
lessons.starterCode:
const app = require('./app');

// Add the 4-argument error handler last
hints: Signature must be `(err, req, res, next)` — all four arguments.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which details of a production error would you keep in the server log but never in the response?

lessons.title: 12. Async errors
lessons.summary: A rejected promise in a handler does not reach Express on its own in Express 4.

activities.title: Catch and forward
activities.instruction: Wrap awaits in `try`/`catch` and call `next(err)`. The error handler then produces the response, so every route fails the same way.

activities.title: Unhandled rejection
activities.question: An async handler awaits a promise that rejects, with no try/catch. What does the client see?
choices: The request hangs until it times out
activities.answer: The request hangs until it times out
activities.explanation: Express 4 does not observe the returned promise, so the rejection becomes an unhandled rejection and the response is never sent.

activities.title: Forward the failure
activities.instruction: Write an async GET `/users/:id` handler that awaits a lookup and forwards any failure with `next(err)`.

teaching.text: Synchronous throws are caught by Express automatically. Rejected promises in Express 4 are not, which is the source of many hung requests.
Express 5 forwards rejected promises for you, but an explicit try/catch still reads better and works on both versions.

lessons.task: Write an async route that forwards failures to the error handler.
lessons.starterCode:
const app = require('./app');

// GET /users/:id — await a lookup, forward errors with next(err)
hints: Accept `next` as the third argument and call `next(err)` from the catch block.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does adding `next` to the handler signature matter for error handling?
